title: A neutral that carries more than the line

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the three lines' ripples fall into step and the neutral bar climb from 0 A past the 150 A line bar near a third, when you drag the third harmonic up.
interactive.title: Three line currents and their neutral
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A refresher lesson in eleven screens on the neutral of a three-phase four-wire circuit whose loads draw harmonic currents. Back and Continue move between the screens. Screen 1, Do you still have it?: “A balanced three-phase load on a four-wire supply draws 60 A in each line. Its maker states a third harmonic of 35% of the line current. What current flows in the neutral?” Three choices, in this order: 0.00 A, 21.00 A, 63.00 A. Right gives “Still there.” and the working: 3 × 0.35 × 60 = 63.00 A,[^1] more than the 60 A in each line. So the neutral current, not the line current, sets the cable.[^2] Then a line on each slip. 0.00 A is true of the fundamentals alone, which cancel.[^3] 21.00 A is one line's third harmonic, 0.35 × 60, and the three lines' third harmonics add.[^4] And 35% is row 3 of Table 4Aa: the neutral current, with a factor of 0.86.[^13] Two buttons follow. Refresh the why goes on to screen 2, and Skip to the practice goes straight to screen 7. Wrong, 0.00 A: a balanced load's fundamentals do cancel in the neutral,[^3][^5] but third harmonic currents add there.[^4] Wrong, 21.00 A: that is one line's third harmonic. The neutral carries all three lines' third harmonics added together,[^6] three times it. Either way, the right working follows and the lesson goes on to screen 2, with no skip. Read: the neutral carries 3 × 0.35 × 60 = 63.00 A, more than a line's 60 A. Screen 2, What it is for: a three-phase circuit is normally designed on its line current. But circuits supplying rectifiers, variable-speed motor drives or fluorescent lighting banks draw currents that are not sinusoidal.[^7] Then the circuit may need designing on the neutral current, not the line current.[^2] A discharge-lighting final circuit must carry its harmonic currents as well as the lamps' current.[^8] In red, if it is skipped: the neutral current adds heat to the cables.[^9] The line currents do not fall to make up for it.[^10] So a cable sized on the line current alone does not allow for that heat. Screen 3, The why: three line currents and their neutral. The opening text says each line current is drawn as two parts. One is a wave at the supply frequency, the fundamental. The other is a smaller wave at three times that frequency, the third harmonic. The picture: at the top, the three line currents, L1, L2 and L3, over one cycle of the supply. Under them is the neutral, their sum at each instant. Under that are two bars on one scale in amperes, Line and Neutral. A slider, Third harmonic, runs from 0 to 50% of the line current in steps of 1% and opens at 0%. Under it, a strip shows Table 4Aa's four rows, with ticks at 15, 33 and 45.[^11][^12][^13][^14] The line current is held at 150 A,[^1] so as the third harmonic's share grows, the fundamental's shrinks. At 0% the three waves are plain sine waves a third of a cycle, 120°, apart. The neutral is flat at 0 A, because balanced fundamentals cancel.[^3] Drag the slider up and each wave gains a ripple at three times the frequency. A bracket between L1's and L2's peaks reads “120° = one ripple cycle”. That 120° is a whole cycle of the ripple, so the three ripples rise and fall together, in phase.[^15] The neutral becomes a wave at three times the supply frequency, the sum of the three.[^6] On the first visit a short demonstration glides the slider from 0% to 35%. Replay runs it again, and coming back to the screen keeps his setting. Readouts: Neutral current, Ibn = 3 × h × IL;[^1] Current that sets the cable, the line's 150 A or the neutral's once it is larger; and the Table 4Aa factor, by row. At 15%, 67.50 A. At 20%, 90.00 A. At 33%, 148.50 A. At 34%, 153.00 A, and the neutral bar passes the line bar and turns red. At 35%, 157.50 A. At 45%, 202.50 A, 135% of the line. At 50%, 225.00 A. On a row's edge, at exactly 15, 33 or 45%, the picture takes the lower row, because the neutral sets the cable only above 33%.[^16] One line under it: the other triple harmonics, the 9th and the 15th, add the same way.[^4] How high a real neutral goes depends on the load. Reported figures run up to 173% of phase current.[^17] Some run up to three times the phase current at the fundamental frequency.[^18] Read: at 0% the neutral carries 0 A. It passes the 150 A line near a third. At 35% it carries 3 × 0.35 × 150 = 157.50 A. Screen 4, Which current, which factor: the current tables are worked for three loaded conductors.[^19] A neutral carrying harmonic current is a fourth loaded conductor in the same cable. BS 7671 Regulation 523.6.1 counts it as one once the third harmonic and its multiples pass 15%.[^20] A neutral carrying only the lines' imbalance is offset by less heat in a line, and the cable is sized on the highest line current.[^21] Harmonic current gets no such offset.[^10] Table 4Aa is drawn as four rows stacked one above the other. Each shows its range, its current and its factor, and is tapped to read its line. 0 to 15%: the line current, factor 1.0.[^11] 15 to 33%: the line current, 0.86.[^12] 33 to 45%: the neutral current, 0.86.[^13] Over 45%: the neutral current, 1.0.[^14] Under the rows, why. Up to 15%, BS 7671 does not yet count the neutral as a loaded conductor, so the line current and a factor of 1.0 stand.[^20] Up to 33% the line is still the larger, so it is Ib. Above 33% the neutral is the larger, and the cable is selected on the neutral current.[^22] The 0.86 is a rating factor for heat the table did not allow for, as in lesson 3.[^23] Here that heat is the fourth loaded conductor's. By 45% the neutral carries 135% of the line. With the cable sized on it, the three lines are not fully loaded,[^24] so the factor goes back to 1.0. A box headed The rule: It ≥ In ÷ (Ca × Cg × the Table 4Aa factor).[^25] Before a device is chosen, divide the current that sets the cable by the factor. That gives the design load.[^26] Then: no neutral, no neutral current.[^30] A three-phase motor often has no neutral connected.[^5] Read: up to 33%, the line current sets the cable, with a factor of 1.0 up to 15% and 0.86 above. Over 33%, the neutral current sets it, with 0.86 up to 45% and 1.0 above. Screen 5, Check: “A three-phase four-wire circuit carries 100 A in each line. The maker's data gives a third harmonic of 50%. What current must its cable be chosen to carry? That is the current that sets it, divided by Table 4Aa's factor.” Choices: 116.28 A, 150.00 A, 174.42 A. Right, 150.00 A: Ibn = 3 × 0.50 × 100 = 150.00 A. That is over 45%, so use the neutral current with a factor of 1.0.[^14] Wrong, 174.42 A, which is 150.00 ÷ 0.86: the 0.86 belongs to the 33 to 45% row. Above 45% the lines are not fully loaded.[^24] Wrong, 116.28 A, which is 100 ÷ 0.86: that is the 15 to 33% row. At 50% the neutral carries 150% of the line, so the cable is selected on it.[^22] Read: 3 × 0.50 × 100 = 150.00 A. That is over 45%, so the factor is 1.0: 150.00 A. Screen 6, Worked example, one line at each press. The text asks him to work each step first, then press Show the next step. The circuit: a harmonic content of 35% and a load of 150 A, in single-core 70 °C thermoplastic cable on Reference Method B. It is grouped with three other circuits at an ambient of 35 °C, and a BS 88-2 fuse protects it. 35% is row 3 of Table 4Aa, so the cable is sized on the neutral current.[^31] Ibn = 3 × 0.35 × 150 = 157.50 A,[^1] more than 150 A, so Ibn is Ib.[^32] In: 160 A, from Fig 3A3(b).[^33] Ca 0.94 at 35 °C. Cg 0.65 for four circuits bunched.[^34] Table 4Aa: 0.86.[^25] 0.94 × 0.65 = 0.611, and 0.611 × 0.86 = 0.52546. It ≥ 160 ÷ 0.52546 = 304.50 A.[^25] Table 4D1A, column 5: 240 mm²,[^35] at 346 A.[^36] Iz = 346 × 0.52546 = 181.81 A, so 157.50 ≤ 160 ≤ 181.81. One line after the last step: if you have seen 304.4 A, that is the same sum cut short. The cable is the same. Read: Ibn = 157.50 A is Ib. In is 160 A. It ≥ 160 ÷ (0.94 × 0.65 × 0.86) = 304.50 A. That gives 240 mm², with Iz 181.81 A. Screen 7, Section A, question 3 (d): the showroom's scenario panel, and parts (a), (b) and (c) carried forward: 4594 W, 8.22 A on L1, and 160.44 A, the installation's maximum demand per phase. The given: DBL2's submain is fed three-phase and four-wire. It has to be, because lesson 2 split its lighting circuits across L1 to L3. Most of its load is the key's fluorescent modular and twin fittings. Take their third harmonic as 20% here; use the maker's figure on a real job. Under it, the maker's figure. Harmonics count only when the maker's data states one.[^27] Then its percentage goes into these sums.[^28] There is no datasheet for the drawing's own fittings. On a real job, no maker's figure means none is applied. So this part shows the method on a practice value. Makers often print total harmonic distortion, THD, instead. THD counts every harmonic, not the third alone. One luminaire datasheet, for example, gives THD 15.00%.[^29] Read which figure the datasheet gives, and say which you used. For scale, IEC 61000-3-2 limits the third harmonic of Class C lighting equipment to 30 × the circuit power factor, in percent.[^40][^41] We apply the 20% to the whole of L1, the heaviest line, 8.22 A, though an LED circuit shares it. That errs on the cautious side. “(d) Using the heaviest line current, determine the neutral current of DBL2's submain.” A typed answer (part 3d): 3 × 0.20 × 8.22 = 4.93 A.[^1] Slips: 1.64 A, which is 0.20 × 8.22, one line's third harmonic; the three add.[^6] 0 A: the fundamentals cancel, but the third harmonics do not.[^4] 24.66 A, which is 3 × 8.22, the share h left out. 8.22 A, the line current. After two misses, the working, and part (e) starts from 4.93 A. Read: Ibn = 3 × 0.20 × 8.22 = 4.93 A, on a practice 20%. That is less than the line's 8.22 A. Screen 8, Section A, question 3 (e): parts (a) to (d) carried forward. “(e) Determine the current DBL2's submain cable must be chosen to carry once Table 4Aa's factor is applied.” A typed answer (part 3e): 20% is the 15 to 33% row, the line current with 0.86,[^12] so 8.22 ÷ 0.86 = 9.56 A. Slips: 8.22 A, the factor left out; at 20% the neutral is a loaded conductor.[^20] 5.73 A, which is 4.93 ÷ 0.86: the neutral is the smaller, and it sets the cable only above 33%.[^16] 7.07 A, which is 8.22 × 0.86: rating factors divide.[^37] After it: 8.22 ÷ 0.86 = 9.56 A is the design load.[^26] Once a device is chosen, In takes Ib's place in It ≥ In ÷ (Ca × Cg × 0.86).[^25] Lesson 8 does that for this submain. So 9.56 A is a floor, not the It the cable is finally chosen on. Then a what-if. Suppose the maker's figure were 35%, as in the worked example, not a showroom figure. Then 3 × 0.35 × 8.22 = 8.63 A, more than 8.22 A, so the neutral would set the cable: 8.63 ÷ 0.86 = 10.03 A. Read: 20% is the 15 to 33% row, so 8.22 ÷ 0.86 = 9.56 A, on a practice 20%. Screen 9, Section B: “Explain why third harmonic currents add in the neutral of a three-phase four-wire circuit, and what that means for the cable.” His written answer is marked against four points. A full answer makes any three, so at least one says what it means for the cable. He gets one more go, then the model answer. Screen 10, Section A, changed numbers, a City & Guilds style question with new numbers: “A three-phase four-wire circuit carries 37 A in each line. The maker's data gives a third harmonic of 40%. Determine the current its cable must be chosen to carry once Table 4Aa's factor is applied.” A typed answer: 3 × 0.40 × 37 = 44.40 A, more than 37 A, so the 33 to 45% row: 44.40 ÷ 0.86 = 51.63 A. Rounded to one place it is 51.6 A, and that is accepted too.[^26] Slips: 44.40 A, the 0.86 left out. 43.02 A, which is 37 ÷ 0.86: the line current, but over 33% the neutral sets the cable. 38.18 A, which is 44.40 × 0.86: the factor divides. Read: 3 × 0.40 × 37 = 44.40 A, and 44.40 ÷ 0.86 = 51.63 A. Screen 11, Keep this: the summary card, then Finish the lesson. The caption under the lesson says practice values are marked and each line is worked from the rounded figure before it. It shows on screens 3 to 8 and 10.
interactive.ignores: Each line current is drawn as a fundamental and a third harmonic only. Real loads also draw the 5th, 7th and higher harmonics. Of those, only the triple ones, such as the 9th and 15th, add in the neutral. The three lines are drawn equal. Real ones differ a little, and the neutral then also carries a small part of the fundamentals. Where the ripple sits against the fundamental is chosen for the drawing. The size of each part, not the shape of the wave, sets the readouts. Table 4Aa's rows are steps, so a figure just across an edge changes the factor at once.

explain.text:
Some loads make the neutral carry more current than any line.[^38] Then the neutral current, not the line current, may have to set the cable.

On a balanced load drawing plain sine-wave currents, the three line currents cancel in the neutral. That is why a balanced motor may have no neutral connected at all. Fluorescent lighting banks, rectifiers and variable-speed drives are different. They draw currents that are not sinusoidal. Part of what they draw does not cancel in the neutral. It adds.

Picture each line current as two waves added together. One runs at the supply frequency: the fundamental. A smaller one runs at three times that frequency: the [[third harmonic]]. On a balanced load the three fundamentals sit a third of a cycle, 120°, apart. So at every instant they add to nothing in the neutral. The third harmonic runs three times as fast. So the same 120° delay is one whole cycle of it. The three lines' third harmonics rise and fall together, in phase. The neutral carries all three added up.

Call each line's third harmonic a share h of its line current IL. Then the neutral carries Ibn = 3 × h × IL.[^1] That passes IL once 3 × h passes 1, so once h passes about a third. A 150 A load at 35% puts 3 × 0.35 × 150 = 157.50 A in the neutral. This picture keeps it simple: three equal lines and the third harmonic alone. The other triple harmonics, such as the 9th, add in the same way.

The current tables assume three loaded conductors. A neutral carrying harmonic current is a fourth [[loaded conductor]], heating the same cable. BS 7671 Regulation 523.6.1 counts it as one once the third harmonic and its multiples pass 15% of the line current.[^20] More heat in the same cable means each conductor reaches its limit at a lower current. So the cable is derated, and that is Table 4Aa's 0.86. Imbalance current in a neutral is different. When the neutral carries it, a line carries less, so the extra heat is offset. Harmonic current in the neutral comes with no such fall in the lines.

Table 4Aa uses the third harmonic to pick both the current and the rating factor.[^12]
- Up to 15%: the line current, factor 1.0.
- 15 to 33%: the line current, factor 0.86.
- 33 to 45%: the neutral current, factor 0.86.
- Over 45%: the neutral current, factor 1.0.

The factor goes back to 1.0 over 45% because the neutral then carries over 135% of the line. With the cable sized on that, the three lines are not fully loaded.[^24] The factor divides In along with the others: It ≥ In ÷ (Ca × Cg × the Table 4Aa factor).[^25] Start from the maker's data. Allow for harmonics only when it gives a figure, and then put that percentage into the sums.

**Once the third harmonic passes about a third of the line current, the neutral carries more than the line. Then the neutral current, Ibn = 3 × h × IL, sets the cable.**

analogy.text: Picture three watches on a ship, each with a day that starts eight hours after the last. Anything each watch does once a day, like taking over, falls at three different times, spread evenly round the clock. Now take something each watch does every eight hours. An eight-hour stagger is one whole lap of that routine. So it falls at the same times for all three. At those times the galley serves all three watches at once: three times one watch's queue.
analogy.breaks: Queues only ever add. Currents have a direction, so the fundamentals can cancel to nothing. And the size of each line's third harmonic comes from the load's electronics, not a rota. So the picture shows why the harmonics line up, not how big they are.

practice.text:
- Ask for the maker's data on each load that draws non-sinusoidal current: fluorescent fittings with their control gear, rectifiers and variable-speed drives. Allow for harmonics only if it gives a figure. Then put that percentage into the sums. Note whether it gives the third harmonic or THD.
- Work the neutral current from the heaviest line current: Ibn = 3 × h × IL.[^1]
- Find the row in Table 4Aa. Up to 15%: the line current, factor 1.0. 15 to 33%: the line current, factor 0.86. 33 to 45%: the neutral current, factor 0.86. Over 45%: the neutral current, factor 1.0.
- Choose In from that current. Then work It ≥ In ÷ (Ca × Cg × the Table 4Aa factor).[^25] Read Table 4D1A's column for three or four cables, three-phase a.c.[^35]
- Check Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz, with Iz worked from the same factors.[^39]

**Rule of thumb:** the neutral overtakes the line once h passes about a third, where 3 × h passes 1. No neutral, no neutral current. So a three-phase motor's cable with no neutral has no neutral to size.

**Worked example:** a 150 A circuit with a third harmonic of 35%. Ibn = 3 × 0.35 × 150 = 157.50 A. That is more than 150 A, so it is Ib. In is 160 A. It ≥ 160 ÷ (0.94 × 0.65 × 0.86) = 160 ÷ 0.52546 = 304.50 A. Cut short instead of rounded, that is 304.4 A, and it gives the same cable. Table 4D1A, column 5, gives 240 mm² at 346 A.[^36] So Iz = 346 × 0.52546 = 181.81 A, and 157.50 ≤ 160 ≤ 181.81.

For the showroom, take a third harmonic of 20% here; use the maker's figure on a real job. DBL2's submain then has Ibn = 3 × 0.20 × 8.22 = 4.93 A. That is below the line's 8.22 A, so the line current sets the cable: 8.22 ÷ 0.86 = 9.56 A.

**Common mistakes**
- Expecting no neutral current because the load is balanced. That is true of the fundamentals only.
- Leaving out the 3 in 3 × h × IL. On its own, h × IL is one line's third harmonic, and the neutral carries all three.
- Sizing on the line current when the third harmonic is over 33%.
- Leaving out the 0.86 between 15 and 45%, or keeping it above 45%.
- Reading a THD figure as the third harmonic without saying so.

b1.q: Explain why third harmonic currents add in the neutral of a three-phase four-wire circuit, and what that means for the cable.

points.text: A balanced load's three fundamental currents are 120° apart, so they cancel in the neutral. A 120° shift is one whole cycle of a wave three times as fast. So the three third harmonics are in phase and do not cancel.

b1.model: In a balanced load the three fundamental currents are 120° apart, so they cancel in the neutral. The third harmonic runs at three times the supply frequency. So the same 120° is one whole cycle of it. The three lines' third harmonics are in phase, so they add. The neutral carries all three: 3 × h × IL. Once the third harmonic passes about a third of the line current, that is more than the line current. Table 4Aa then sizes the cable on the neutral current. Above 15% the neutral also counts as a fourth loaded conductor, adding heat to the cable. The current tables assume three loaded conductors, so they do not allow for it. That is why Table 4Aa applies a factor of 0.86 between 15% and 45%.

summary.title: A neutral that carries more than the line
summary.for: Fluorescent lighting, rectifiers and drives draw current that is not a clean sine wave. Their third harmonics add in the neutral, which can then carry more than a line. Table 4Aa tells you which current sets the cable, and what factor to apply.
summary.rule:
Ibn = 3 × h × IL (h: the third harmonic as a share of the line current)
0 to 15%: line current, factor 1.0
15 to 33%: line current, factor 0.86
33 to 45%: neutral current, factor 0.86
over 45%: neutral current, factor 1.0
It ≥ In ÷ (Ca × Cg × the Table 4Aa factor)

Use it only when the maker's data gives a harmonic figure. Say whether it is the third harmonic or THD.
Balanced fundamentals cancel in the neutral. Third harmonics add.
No neutral, no neutral current.
